newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bombs kill 13 in Jerusalem, Israel slams Arafat.
newsitem.headline: Bombs kill 13 in Jerusalem, Israel slams Arafat.

text.p: Thirteen people were killed and 157 wounded on Wednesday when two Arab suicide bombers blew themselves up in a crowded market in the heart of Jewish West Jerusalem, police said.
The bombings were the deadliest single attack on the Jewish state since March 1996 and cast strong doubt over prospects for a resumption in stalled Israeli-Palestinian peace talks.

U.S. envoy Dennis Ross had been due in the region on Thursday to put "new ideas" to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat on ways to end the impasse but postponed the trip after the attack.
"The Israelis are mourning their people. We'll postpone it until it is appropriate," a White House spokesman said.
The bombs tore through the popular Mahane Yehuda market, crowded with lunchtime shoppers, within seconds of each other at 1:18 p.m. (1018 GMT), sowing carnage and panic.
Blood mixed on the ground with pulverised produce as police, emergency workers and members of the public struggled to remove the dead and get the injured to hospitals.
"There were two large explosions and then I saw body parts flying in the air. There was a big fireball right in my face," one witness said.

U.S. President Bill Clinton joined France and Germany, key players in Europe's efforts to promote agreement, in condemning the attack, coupling their outrage with appeals not to let the killings derail the drive for peace.
But a senior aide to Netanyahu said it would be virtually impossible to negotiate peace with the Palestinian Authority unless it "changed its attitude to terrorism".

"The world will have to realise and the Palestinian Authority will have to realise that it is either violence and terrorism or a peace process. They cannot have it both ways," communications chief David Bar-Illan told Reuters.
Another official said Netanyahu had received a telephone call of condolence from Arafat but told the Palestinian leader in a "very tough conversation" that sorrow would not suffice.

"The prime minister told him...that he is not satisfied with an expression of sorrow and that he demands Arafat act resolutely against the terrorist organisations and their infrastructure," Israeli spokesman Shai Bazak said.

Police initially put the death toll at 18 but later lowered the figure to 13, including the two bombers. There was no immediate claim of responsibility. Moslem militant groups have carried out past attacks that have killed scores of Israelis.

"It was a coordinated attack by two suicide bombers. I think we've never seen such an incident where two suicide terrorists coordinate their attack in the same spot. This is definitely something new," police chief Assaf Hefetz said.

Police said they had arrested three right-wing Israeli activists near the market, where Jewish demonstrators gathered to chant "Death to Arabs" and slogans against Netanyahu, elected last year on a promise to stop suicide attacks.
Authorities also imposed a closure on the West Bank and Gaza Strip, barring Palestinians from entering Israel and army radio said Israelis had been barred from Palestinian self-rule areas.

The radio quoted Shin Bet security service officials as saying the bombers, dressed smartly to appear as businessmen, had smuggled two 10-kilo (22-pound) bombs into parallel streets in the market in attach cases.
The blasts were the bloodiest single attack in Israel since March 3, 1996 when a suicide bomb blast in a bus in Jerusalem killed at least 18 people.
The last big bombing to rock the Jewish state, on March 21, killed three Israeli women along with the Palestinian bomber, and wounded 42 people at an outdoor cafe in Tel Aviv.
That attack happened three days after Israel broke ground on a Jewish settlement on a hilltop in Arab East Jerusalem known to Israelis as Har Homa and to Palestinians as Jabal Abu Ghneim.
Israeli-Palestinian peace talks have been in crisis since then, with Arafat insisting substantive talks on a final peace agreement cannot take place until settlement activity stops.
Israel has countered that the Palestinian Authority has failed to meet commitments made under interim peace deals since 1993 to stem violence against Israelis.

Israel recently arrested four Palestinian police officers who it said planned to attack Jewish settlers in the West Bank. It has accused the chief of Palestinian police of involvement in the alleged plan.
Arafat has said he was making a "100 percent effort" to stop Palestinian attacks in Israel but could not guarantee complete success.
One of his senior negotiators, Saeb Erekat, said Wednesday's killings should not be allowed to wreck peace efforts.
"The answer should be the strong message that they will not win, extremists on both sides. People who commit terror will not win and the peace process must continue," he said.
